---
title: "Quiz: Kinds of files"
---

[Lecture](../lectures/01-files/lec.qmd) · [Exercises](01-files.qmd)

Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

---

**Q1.** Which of these are plain-text files: `seedlings.csv`, `report.Rmd`, `seedling-notes.docx`, `dna.txt`, `seedlings.xlsx`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which of them would show readable words and numbers, and nothing else, in Notepad or TextEdit?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`seedlings.csv`, `report.Rmd` and `dna.txt` are plain text. `seedling-notes.docx` and `seedlings.xlsx` are compressed ZIP packages that need a word processor or spreadsheet program.
:::

---

**Q2.** You open a `.docx` file in a text editor and see `PK` followed by strange symbols. Is the file damaged?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is a `.docx` file really, underneath?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. A `.docx` is a ZIP package of XML files, so a text editor shows raw bytes. Copy it, rename the copy to `.zip` and extract it: the text is in `word/document.xml`.
:::

---

**Q3.** The first lines of a CSV are:

```text
plant_id,treatment,initial_mm,final_mm
P01,control,25.7,44.3
```

How many plant records are shown? How much did P01 grow?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The first line names the columns. Growth is final length minus initial length.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One plant record; the header is not a plant. P01 grew `44.3 - 25.7 = 18.6` mm.
:::

---

**Q4.** Name two things an Excel file can store that a CSV file cannot. Why does this course still keep data as CSV?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of what you saw in `examples/seedlings.xlsx`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Formatting (bold or coloured cells), formulas, and several sheets. CSV stores values only, but any program, including R and a text editor, can read it, and what you see is exactly what is stored.
:::

---

**Q5.** A gene list contains `SEPT2` and `MARCH1`. A colleague opens it in Excel, saves it, and sends it on. What may have gone wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do `SEPT` and `MARCH` look like to a spreadsheet?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Excel may have turned them into dates such as `2-Sep` and `1-Mar`, and saving made that permanent. About one in five published papers with Excel gene lists contained such errors (Ziemann et al. 2016). The genes are now called `SEPTIN2` and `MARCHF1`.
:::

---

**Q6.** A classmate's CSV contains the line `P01;control;25,7;44,3`. What is different from the course file, and where does such a file come from?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look at what separates the values, and at the decimal sign.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Values are separated by semicolons and decimals use a comma (25,7 instead of 25.7). Excel set to Swedish (and many other European languages) saves "CSV" this way. Programs expecting commas will split the rows in the wrong places, so always look at a CSV in a text editor first.
:::

---

**Q7.** You paste `read.csv(“data/seedlings.csv”)` from a Word document into R and get `Error: unexpected input`. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look closely at the quote marks.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Word replaced the straight quotes `"` with curly quotes `“ ”`, which R does not understand. Write code in a text editor or RStudio.
:::

---

**Q8.** You rename `seedlings.csv` to `seedlings.xlsx`. Is it now an Excel file?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does renaming rewrite the contents?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. The contents are still plain text with commas; only the label changed, and Excel will refuse to open it. Converting a format needs a program that rewrites the file, such as **Save As**.
:::
